g.title: same character as kěyǐ / 可以

This sentence starts with 可/kě is used here as a shortened, spoken form of 但是/dànshì or 可是/kěshì, meaning "but" or "however". Gemini informs: what makes this sentence work so well is the relationship between 可/kě at the beginning and 就是/jiùshì in the middle: 可 flags to the listener: "Pay attention, a problem is coming!" 说明/就是 emphasizes the total frustration or helplessness of the situation: "He tried, but he just couldn't do it." If you were reading this fable out loud, that initial 可 is the exact moment the tension spikes for the character! · The three characters 干就是 gàn jiù shì seem to form two words, either gànjiù and jiùshì with different meanings. Gemini points out the role of jiùshì to mean "just", while the translation suggests that gànjiù/just do it is more appropriate. So these three altogether form a hybrid or emphasis where the binding is ambiguous.

g.title: This sentence contains two "lin" words. In the first half of the sentence, lín is the character 林. The Word: 树林 i.e. shùlín with literal meaning 树 /shù / tree + 林 / lín / forest/grove. Character Origin: the character 林, it is literally made of two "tree" characters 木 = mù standing side-by-side. In the second half of the sentence, lín is the character 临 [traditional: 臨]. The Word: 来临 / láilín has literal meaning 来 / lái / to come + 临 / to arrive/draw near. Usage: 临 on its own means "to be close to," "to face," or "to arrive." When combined as 来临, it means "to arrive" or "to approach." It is highly formal and usually used for abstract things, e.g., danger approaching, winter arriving, or a new era coming. · This sentence contains two "jiu" words: 不久 /bù jiǔ / not long after, and 就 / jiù / then or immediately.
